props.title: Brainstorm
props.initialSlug: Scientists create device to record human experiences

sections.content: Brainstorm (1983) represents a fascinating intersection of technological ambition and tragic Hollywood history. Douglas Trumbull, fresh off groundbreaking visual effects work for 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) and Close Encounters of the Third Kind (1977), directed this prescient sci-fi thriller about recording and experiencing human memories. The film's pioneering use of 70mm Showscan process aimed to revolutionize how audiences experienced movies, similar to how Avatar (2009) would later push 3D boundaries. Tragically, star Natalie Wood's death during production nearly derailed the entire project, with MGM initially wanting to scrap the film. Christopher Walken and producer Lloyd Kaufman fought to complete Wood's final film.

sections.content: The film's exploration of transferring human consciousness and memories predates similar themes in later sci-fi classics like Strange Days (1995) and Inception (2010). Trumbull's practical effects work, especially the memory playback sequences, holds up remarkably well. The film's innovative split-screen technique used different aspect ratios to distinguish reality from recorded memories - a technical achievement that influenced later films like Interstellar (2014) in depicting subjective experiences.

Beyond its technical innovations, Brainstorm tackles ethical questions about technology that feel eerily relevant today. Like The Lawnmower Man (1992) and Transcendence (2014), it warns about the military-industrial complex corrupting breakthrough technologies. The addiction subplot, where characters become hooked on experiencing others' memories, anticipates modern debates about social media and virtual reality dependence. sections.content: Douglas Trumbull's determination to push cinema technology forward with Brainstorm deserves special attention. His Showscan process, filming at 60 frames per second on 70mm film, was decades ahead of its time. Similar high-frame-rate experiments wouldn't return until Peter Jackson's The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey (2012). The film's blend of practical effects and ambitious narrative scope influenced later directors like Christopher Nolan, whose Inception (2010) similarly explored the intersection of technology and consciousness.
